Performing initial audit of PKGBUILD to ensure that we can safely run `makepkg`
LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD defines standard source URLs that point to GitHub releases for the project, specific to each architecture. The sources are downloaded via HTTPS from the declared upstream (github.com/jpillora/binid), which is appropriate and expected. The `sha256sums` are explicitly provided for both architectures and are not set to 'SKIP', so integrity verification will occur during source download. No command substitution, `pkgver()` function, or top-level code outside of variable assignments is present, meaning no arbitrary code execution will occur when sourcing the PKGBUILD during `makepkg --printsrcinfo` or `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare`.

The `source` array uses variable expansions but does not include any suspicious constructs such as `$(curl ...)`, `$(wget ...)`, or `eval`. The file contains only static declarations, and all network activity is limited to fetching the defined release binaries and verifying them against shipped checksums. Since no functions like `prepare()`, `build()`, or `package()` are executed under these flags, and no dynamic code runs at parse time, there is no risk of malicious behavior during this phase.
</details>
<evidence>

</evidence>
<summary>
No dynamic code or malicious fetches in PKGBUILD scope</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD file defines a standard Arch Linux package for `binid-bin`, a tool for cryptographic binary identification. It fetches prebuilt binary releases from the project's official GitHub repository (`https://github.com/jpillora/binid`) using versioned release URLs, which ensures that the source is traceable and matches the declared upstream. The package uses proper checksums (sha256sums) for both supported architectures (x86_64 and aarch64), and the checksums are not set to 'SKIP', indicating verified integrity.

The build process is minimal and appropriate: it extracts the downloaded tarball (handled automatically by makepkg due to the `.tar.gz` extension) and installs the binary, README, and license file to standard system locations. There are no suspicious operations such as network calls, file obfuscation, execution of downloaded code, or system modifications outside the package directory. The use of `!strip` is justified since the binary is precompiled and stripping may be unnecessary or even harmful depending on the binary format.

All operations align with standard AUR packaging practices for a `-bin` package distributing a prebuilt release. The maintainer does not modify the upstream code, and the sources are fetched over HTTPS from a trusted and relevant domain (github.com/jpillora/binid). No evidence of malicious behavior, backdoors, or supply-chain attacks was found.
</details>
<evidence>

Standard -bin package with verified prebuilt binaries</summary>
</security_assessment>

The file defines a single source for the `binid-bin` package, specifying that it should track the latest release from the GitHub repository `jpillora/binid` with version tags prefixed by "v". This is a standard and legitimate use of nvchecker.

There is no executable code, no network operations beyond what is expected from version checking, and no suspicious commands or data exfiltration mechanisms. The configuration only instructs nvchecker to poll a public GitHub repository for new releases, which is a common and safe practice in AUR package maintenance. No obfuscation, unexpected downloads, or system modifications are present.

The repository referenced (`jpillora/binid`) appears to be the legitimate upstream for the `binid` tool, and tracking its latest release is consistent with packaging best practices for binary distributions. No malicious behavior or supply-chain risks are evident in this file.

The content promotes legitimate cryptographic use cases such as signing binaries with Ed25519 keys, embedding metadata, and enabling self-validation in Go programs.

One notable installation method uses a curl-to-bash pattern: `curl "https://i.jpillora.com/binid" | bash`. The README itself does not host malicious instructions; it merely documents an existing installation workflow. Users are expected to evaluate such installation methods based on their own security policies.

All described functionality aligns with the stated purpose of binary identification and integrity verification.
